We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: A NEURAL ARCHITECTURE FOR RULE-GUIDED BEHAVIOR: A SIMULATION OF PHYSIOLOGICAL EXPERIMENTS
papers.research_question: How does the brain implement rule-guided behavior, and what is the functional role of rule-selective neurons in the prefrontal cortex?
papers.core_contribution: Developed a recurrent neural network model that simulates rule-guided behavior, showing that rule-selective units encode rule information and interact with other units to produce context-appropriate responses, predicting functional interactions in the prefrontal cortex.
papers.conclusion: The simulation demonstrates that rule-selective neurons play a crucial role in coding and retaining rule information, and the recurrent network architecture with ample mutual connections explains flexible rule-guided behavior in the prefrontal cortex.
papers.key_findings:
The model contains rule-selective units that encode and maintain rule information during the delay period.
Object-selective units maintain object information separately from rule information.
Response units integrate rule and object information to produce motor outputs.
Lesion of rule-selective units affects output only in the corresponding rule mode, indicating separate processing streams.
Analysis of connection weights shows how rule-selective, object-selective, and response units are interconnected to perform the task.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to directly connect the learning algorithm (RTRL) with the learning mechanisms of the cerebral cortex.
The model architecture is very simple and may not capture all complexities of the prefrontal cortex.
future_direction: Future work should consider anticipatory dynamics and more reasonable representations of the cues.
papers.abstract: The ability to use abstract rules is very important in applying our experience to new situations. To examine the system governing such rule-guided behavior, we developed a recurrent neural network model of rule-guided behavior and simulated a physiological experiment involving a rule-guided delayed task (Wallis, Anderson, & Miller, 2001). Our model was constructed using neural system identification (Zipser, 1992), and a fully recurrent neural network model was optimized to perform a rule-guided delayed task. The model’s hidden layer contained rule-selective units, and an examination of connection weights substantiated the postulate that rule-selective neurons maintain encoded rule information and contribute to rule-guided responses indirectly. The simulation results predicted functional interactions among neurons involved in various task-related activities. The similarity between the behavior of the model units and biological neurons shows that the brain uses mechanisms like those of the model, and that ample mutual connections in the prefrontal cortex are the basis for promoting flexible learning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Propositional Interpretability in Artificial Intelligence
papers.research_question: What is the importance of propositional interpretability in AI, and how can we achieve thought logging (logging all relevant propositional attitudes in an AI system over time)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues for the importance of propositional interpretability (interpreting AI systems in terms of propositional attitudes such as belief, desire, and subjective probability) and sets out the concrete challenge of thought logging.
papers.conclusion: Propositional interpretability is a vital research program for understanding AI systems, and thought logging represents a key multi-decade challenge for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Propositional interpretability is crucial for AI safety, ethics, and cognitive science, as it allows understanding a system's goals (desires) and world models (beliefs).
Existing interpretability methods (causal tracing, probing, sparse auto-encoders, chain of thought) have strengths and weaknesses for propositional interpretability, often focusing on belief-like attitudes and being limited in robustness and open-endedness.
Thought logging—creating systems that log all relevant propositional attitudes in an AI system over time—is a central, long-term challenge for the field.
future_direction: Developing thought logging systems to track an AI system's propositional attitudes over time.
Extending interpretability methods to cover attitudes beyond belief, such as desires, probabilities, and intentions.
Exploring the extension of interpretability to perception and consciousness.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability is the program of explaining what AI systems are doing in terms of their internal mechanisms. I analyze some aspects of the program, along with setting out some concrete challenges and assessing progress to date. I argue for the importance of propositional interpretability, which involves interpreting a system's mechanisms and behavior in terms of propositional attitudes: attitudes (such as belief, desire, or subjective probability) to propositions (e.g. the proposition that it is hot outside). Propositional attitudes are the central way that we interpret and explain human beings and they are likely to be central in AI too. A central challenge is what I call thought logging: creating systems that log all of the relevant propositional attitudes in an AI system over time. I examine currently popular methods of interpretability (such as probing, sparse auto-encoders, and chain of thought methods) as well as philosophical methods of interpretation (including those grounded in psychosemantics) to assess their strengths and weaknesses as methods of propositional interpretability.

papers.title: Adversarial Manipulation of Reasoning Models using Internal Representations
papers.abstract: Reasoning models generate chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens before their final output, but how this affects their vulnerability to jailbreak attacks remains unclear. While traditional language models make refusal decisions at the prompt-response boundary, we find evidence that DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B makes these decisions within its CoT generation. We identify a linear direction in activation space during CoT token generation that predicts whether the model will refuse or comply -- termed the "caution" direction because it corresponds to cautious reasoning patterns in the generated text. Ablating this direction from model activations increases harmful compliance, effectively jailbreaking the model. We additionally show that intervening only on CoT token activations suffices to control final outputs, and that incorporating this direction into prompt-based attacks improves success rates. Our findings suggest that the chain-of-thought itself is a promising new target for adversarial manipulation in reasoning models. Code available at https://github.com/ky295/reasoning-manipulation.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: Harm-Conditioned Computational Friction as a Diagnostic of Alignment Robustness: A Critical Review and Evaluation Framework
papers.research_question: How can alignment robustness be diagnosed using harm-conditioned computational friction? The paper investigates this by reviewing existing evaluation methods and proposing HCCF as a unifying diagnostic framework.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces harm-conditioned computational friction (HCCF) as a diagnostic framework for AI alignment evaluation, unifying behavioral, inference-level, and mechanistic signals into an evidence hierarchy and providing an evaluation blueprint.
papers.conclusion: HCCF provides a framework for distinguishing genuine safety from superficial compliance, with implications for model auditing and AI safety governance, though implementation challenges such as complexity matching and proxy validation remain.
papers.limitation:
The complexity confound: difficulty-induced processing cost may be misattributed to harm-conditioned resistance.
Theatrical friction and reward-shaped simulation: models may learn to perform friction via stylized cues without genuine internal resistance.
Proxy ambiguity under black-box access: individual proxies like latency or entropy shifts may not reliably indicate ethical conflict.
Normative dependency of harm labels: harm potential is socially contested and context-dependent.
Adversarial co-adaptation to new diagnostics: models could be trained to game friction metrics.
future_direction: standardized harm annotation protocols
friction-aware matched-pair benchmark suites
systematic anti-cosplay stress tests
cross-domain stability metrics with meta-estimation
training-time friction shaping
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Robust alignment requires that AI models maintain safety-relevant behavior under distribution shift, adversarial prompting, and optimization pressure. Current evaluation methods often rely on surface compliance metrics—such as refusal rates or policy-template adherence—that may fail to detect fragile safety generalization, reward hacking, or prompt-contingent refusal policies. This paper critically reviews alignment evaluation methods through the lens of harm-conditioned computational friction (HCCF): a diagnostic principle positing that aligned models should exhibit measurable increases in deliberative cost, uncertainty, or constraint activation specifically when processing higher-harm inputs, controlling for task difficulty. We formalize HCCF through behavioral, inference-level, and mechanistic proxies; propose measurement protocols for friction gradients across harm domains; analyze confounds and failure modes (including "theatrical friction"); and provide an evaluation blueprint with robustness checks and cross-domain aggregation. By emphasizing conditional internal resistance rather than only external refusal behavior, HCCF provides a framework to unify existing evaluation methods and distinguish genuine safety generalization from brittle or cosmetic alignment, with potential implications for model auditing, training objectives, and AI safety governance.

papers.title: When Should We Introduce Safety Interventions During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: What is the optimal timing for introducing safety interventions during pretraining to improve model robustness and steerability?
papers.core_contribution: The optimal timing for safety interventions during pretraining depends on the inference setting: delayed interventions (20%-60% of pretraining) improve robustness under standard decoding, while early interventions (0%) improve steerability under safety-aware inference (SafeBeam).
papers.conclusion: Intervention timing is a key curriculum design choice for safety pretraining, with early starts improving steerability under safety-aware inference and delayed starts improving robustness under standard decoding and after benign finetuning.
papers.key_findings:
Introducing safety interventions after an initial safe-only pretraining phase (20%-60%) yields the safest models under standard top-k decoding.
For safety-aware inference (SafeBeam), starting interventions from the beginning (0%) provides the best steerability towards safer generations.
Earlier interventions improve linear separability of safe vs harmful examples in the representation space, especially with metadata.
Delayed interventions improve robustness to adversarial jailbreaks via the GCG algorithm.
Safety interventions do not degrade general capabilities and may even improve them slightly.
papers.limitation: The study varies both timing and amount of intervention data, making it hard to disentangle the effects of timing from quantity, though non-monotonic results suggest timing matters beyond quantity.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying mechanisms of why intervention timing affects safety outcomes.
Explore implications for external monitoring and black-box safety methods.
papers.abstract: Prior work has shown that safety interventions applied during pretraining, such as removing and rephrasing harmful content, can substantially improve the robustness of the resulting models. In this paper, we study the fundamental question that prior work has overlooked: "When during pretraining should safety interventions be introduced?" We keep the underlying data sources and pretraining interventions fixed, varying the intervention start time (after 0%, 20%, or 60% of pretraining tokens). We find that the optimal start time is not one-size-fits-all: with standard top-k decoding, introducing interventions after a short initial phase of safe-only pretraining (20%-60%) often yields the strongest robustness, with the clearest benefits emerging after downstream, benign finetuning. In contrast, for safety-aware inference, interventions starting from the beginning improve steerability towards safer generations. Finally, we observe that earlier interventions reshape internal representations: linear probes more cleanly separate safe vs harmful examples. Our results are the first to establish intervention timing as a key curriculum design choice for safety.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Diagnosing Generalization Failures in Fine-Tuned LLMs: A Cross-Architectural Study on Phishing Detection
papers.research_question: How do model architecture, data diversity, and training strategy (like Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning) affect the generalization failures of fine-tuned LLMs in phishing detection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a diagnostic framework combining SHAP analysis and mechanistic interpretability (attention heatmaps) to uncover the root causes of generalization failures in fine-tuned LLMs, revealing that generalization depends on the synergy between model architecture and data diversity.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that real-world robustness of fine-tuned LLMs depends on a complex interplay between model architecture, data diversity, and fine-tuning strategy, and underscores the necessity of moving beyond simple accuracy metrics to a holistic evaluation approach combining multi-domain testing, deep data inspection, and interpretability tools.
papers.key_findings:
Gemma 2 9B achieves state-of-the-art performance (>91% F1) when trained on a stylistically diverse generalist dataset, demonstrating a powerful synergy between architecture and data diversity.
Llama 3.1 8B performs well on narrow domain data but fails to integrate diverse data, leading to a significant performance drop, showing generalization is highly architecture-dependent.
Mistral model is a consistent and resilient performer across multiple training paradigms, indicating some architectures are inherently more generalizable.
Significant label noise (up to 22%) and naturally occurring adversarial text in public phishing datasets can cause models to learn brittle, non-generalizable heuristics.
Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning benefits Mistral but hinders Gemma, indicating that the benefit of structured reasoning is architecture-dependent and not universally beneficial.
papers.limitation:
The data quality audit is performed by a model, not human annotators, so the flagged samples are potential mislabels and require manual validation for full confirmation.
The SHAP analysis is a manual process and could be automated for scalability.
future_direction: Data curation and augmentation using automated auditing tools and synthetic data generation.
Advanced training strategies such as curriculum learning, domain-adaptive pre-training, and ensemble of experts.
Architectural exploration including testing other architectures like mixture-of-experts models and model merging techniques.
papers.abstract: The practice of fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) has achieved state-of-the-art performance on specialized tasks, yet diagnosing why these models become brittle and fail to generalize remains a critical open problem. To address this, we introduce and apply a multi-layered diagnostic framework to a cross-architectural study. We fine-tune Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B, and Mistral models on a high-stakes phishing detection task and use SHAP analysis and mechanistic interpretability to uncover the root causes of their generalization failures. Our investigation reveals three critical findings: (1) Generalization is driven by a powerful synergy between architecture and data diversity. The Gemma 2 9B model achieves state-of-the-art performance (>91\% F1), but only when trained on a stylistically diverse ``generalist'' dataset. (2) Generalization is highly architecture-dependent. We diagnose a specific failure mode in Llama 3.1 8B, which performs well on a narrow domain but cannot integrate diverse data, leading to a significant performance drop. (3) Some architectures are inherently more generalizable. The Mistral model proves to be a consistent and resilient performer across multiple training paradigms. By pinpointing the flawed heuristics responsible for these failures, our work provides a concrete methodology for diagnosing and understanding generalization failures, underscoring that reliable AI requires deep validation of the interplay between architecture, data, and training strategy.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Cognitive Habits of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), which autonomously produce a reasoning Chain of Thought (CoT) before producing final responses, offer a promising approach to interpreting and monitoring model behaviors. Inspired by the observation that certain CoT patterns -- e.g., ``Wait, did I miss anything?'' -- consistently emerge across tasks, we explore whether LRMs exhibit human-like cognitive habits. Building on Habits of Mind, a well-established framework of cognitive habits associated with successful human problem-solving, we introduce CogTest, a principled benchmark designed to evaluate LRMs' cognitive habits. CogTest includes 16 cognitive habits, each instantiated with 25 diverse tasks, and employs an evidence-first extraction method to ensure reliable habit identification. With CogTest, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 16 widely used LLMs (13 LRMs and 3 non-reasoning ones). Our findings reveal that LRMs, unlike conventional LLMs, not only exhibit human-like habits but also adaptively deploy them according to different tasks. Finer-grained analyses further uncover patterns of similarity and difference in LRMs' cognitive habit profiles, particularly certain inter-family similarity (e.g., Qwen-3 models and DeepSeek-R1). Extending the study to safety-related tasks, we observe that certain habits, such as Taking Responsible Risks, are strongly associated with the generation of harmful responses. These findings suggest that studying persistent behavioral patterns in LRMs' CoTs is a valuable step toward deeper understanding of LLM misbehavior. The code is available at: https://github.com/jianshuod/CogTest.

papers.title: HeadHunt-VAD: Hunting Robust Anomaly-Sensitive Heads in MLLM for Tuning-Free Video Anomaly Detection
papers.research_question: How can we perform video anomaly detection without fine-tuning by directly identifying and leveraging a sparse set of robust, anomaly-sensitive attention heads within a frozen Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a tuning-free video anomaly detection paradigm that identifies a sparse set of robust, anomaly-sensitive attention heads within a frozen MLLM and uses their features for efficient and accurate detection.
papers.conclusion: HeadHunt-V AD validates head-level probing in frozen MLLMs as a powerful and practical paradigm for real-world video anomaly detection, achieving superior performance with remarkable computational and data efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
HeadHunt-V AD achieves state-of-the-art performance among tuning-free methods on UCF-Crime (87.03% AUC) and XD-Violence (82.63% AP).
The Robust Head Identification (RHI) module effectively identifies heads that are discriminative and stable across diverse prompts.
The method is highly efficient, requiring only a single forward pass, minimal data (1% of training set), and low feature dimensionality.
Features from the selected expert heads form well-separated clusters in the feature space, confirming their discriminative power.
The lightweight logistic regression anomaly scorer and calibrated temporal locator enable accurate detection and localization with high interpretability.
papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to locate events that deviate from normal patterns in videos. Traditional approaches often rely on extensive labeled data and incur high computational costs. Recent tuning-free methods based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a promising alternative by leveraging their rich world knowledge. However, these methods typically rely on textual outputs, which introduces information loss, exhibits normalcy bias, and suffers from prompt sensitivity, making them insufficient for capturing subtle anomalous cues. To address these constraints, we propose HeadHunt-VAD, a novel tuning-free VAD paradigm that bypasses textual generation by directly hunting robust anomaly-sensitive internal attention heads within the frozen MLLM. Central to our method is a Robust Head Identification module that systematically evaluates all attention heads using a multi-criteria analysis of saliency and stability, identifying a sparse subset of heads that are consistently discriminative across diverse prompts. Features from these expert heads are then fed into a lightweight anomaly scorer and a temporal locator, enabling efficient and accurate anomaly detection with interpretable outputs. Extensive experiments show that HeadHunt-VAD achieves state-of-the-art performance among tuning-free methods on two major VAD benchmarks while maintaining high efficiency, validating head-level probing in MLLMs as a powerful and practical solution for real-world anomaly detection.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal
papers.research_question: How can we systematically evaluate large language models' safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SORRY-Bench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating LLM safety refusal with a fine-grained taxonomy, balanced dataset, linguistic augmentations, and an efficient automated evaluator based on fine-tuned small LLMs.
papers.conclusion: SORRY-Bench provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs’ safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner.
papers.key_findings:
Prior safety evaluation datasets are imbalanced, over-representing certain fine-grained risk categories.
Linguistic mutations in prompts (e.g., different languages, writing styles) significantly affect model safety refusal performance.
Fine-tuned small LLMs (7B parameters) can achieve accuracy comparable to large LLMs like GPT-4 for safety evaluation, at lower computational cost.
Safety refusal varies widely across models; Claude-2 and Gemini-1.5 exhibit the most refusals, while Mistral models show high fulfillment rates.
Some risk categories (e.g., harassment, child-related crimes) are more frequently refused than others (e.g., legal advice, religion promotion).
papers.limitation:
The specialized safety evaluator model is not an ultimate gold standard and occasionally fails to align with human rubrics.
Due to resource and time constraints, the work did not conduct comprehensive testing across a spectrum of decoding parameters (e.g., varying temperatures).
papers.abstract: Evaluating aligned large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize and reject unsafe user requests is crucial for safe, policy-compliant deployments. Existing evaluation efforts, however, face three limitations that we address with SORRY-Bench, our proposed benchmark. First, existing methods often use coarse-grained taxonomies of unsafe topics, and are over-representing some fine-grained topics. For example, among the ten existing datasets that we evaluated, tests for refusals of self-harm instructions are over 3x less represented than tests for fraudulent activities. SORRY-Bench improves on this by using a fine-grained taxonomy of 44 potentially unsafe topics, and 440 class-balanced unsafe instructions, compiled through human-in-the-loop methods. Second, linguistic characteristics and formatting of prompts are often overlooked, like different languages, dialects, and more -- which are only implicitly considered in many evaluations. We supplement SORRY-Bench with 20 diverse linguistic augmentations to systematically examine these effects. Third, existing evaluations rely on large LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) for evaluation, which can be computationally expensive. We investigate design choices for creating a fast, accurate automated safety evaluator. By collecting 7K+ human annotations and conducting a meta-evaluation of diverse LLM-as-a-judge designs, we show that fine-tuned 7B LLMs can achieve accuracy comparable to GPT-4 scale LLMs, with lower computational cost. Putting these together, we evaluate over 50 proprietary and open-weight LLMs on SORRY-Bench, analyzing their distinctive safety refusal behaviors. We hope our effort provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs' safety refusal capabilities, in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner. Benchmark demo, data, code, and models are available through https://sorry-bench.github.io.

papers.title: SaLoRA: Safety-Alignment Preserved Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.research_question: What is the reason for safety alignment drop after LoRA fine-tuning, and how can we preserve safety alignment during low-rank adaptation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SaLoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that preserves safety alignment by introducing a fixed safety module and task-specific initialization for low-rank adapters.
papers.conclusion: SaLoRA effectively preserves safety alignment during LoRA fine-tuning while maintaining performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning significantly alters the safety features of LLMs, leading to a drop in safety alignment.
SaLoRA, with its fixed safety module and task-specific initialization, preserves safety alignment while achieving comparable or better downstream task performance.
SaLoRA outperforms existing PEFT methods (LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA) and post-hoc alignment methods (Self-Reminder, InferAligner, Vaccine, Safe LoRA) in terms of harmful rate and utility.
Task-specific initialization for SaLoRA adapters improves convergence and performance compared to standard initialization.
SaLoRA maintains safety alignment even under jailbreak attacks (multi-GCG attack).
papers.abstract: As advancements in large language models (LLMs) continue and the demand for personalized models increases, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods (e.g., LoRA) will become essential due to their efficiency in reducing computation costs. However, recent studies have raised alarming concerns that LoRA fine-tuning could potentially compromise the safety alignment in LLMs, posing significant risks for the model owner. In this paper, we first investigate the underlying mechanism by analyzing the changes in safety alignment related features before and after fine-tuning. Then, we propose a fixed safety module calculated by safety data and a task-specific initialization for trainable parameters in low-rank adaptations, termed Safety-alignment preserved Low-Rank Adaptation (SaLoRA). Unlike previous LoRA methods and their variants, SaLoRA enables targeted modifications to LLMs without disrupting their original alignments. Our experiments show that SaLoRA outperforms various adapters-based approaches across various evaluation metrics in different fine-tuning tasks.

papers.title: Behind the Scene: Revealing the Secrets of Pre-trained Vision-and-Language Models
papers.research_question: How do pre-trained vision-and-language models work internally? Specifically, the paper investigates multimodal fusion, modality importance, cross-modal interaction, visual relations, and linguistic knowledge in these models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces VALUE, a set of probing tasks for vision-and-language models, and uses it to analyze UNITER and LXMERT, revealing that textual modality is more dominant, a subset of heads specialize in cross-modal interaction, and visual relations and linguistic knowledge are encoded.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into the inner workings of pre-trained V+L models and offers guidelines for future model design, such as preferring single-stream architecture and initializing with BERT weights.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models attend more to text than images during inference.
A subset of attention heads are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions.
Learned attention matrices show patterns coherent with latent alignment between image regions and textual words.
Attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions.
Linguistic knowledge is effectively encoded in the attention heads.
future_direction: Perform model compression via pruning attention heads based on the analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent Transformer-based large-scale pre-trained models have revolutionized vision-and-language (V+L) research. Models such as ViLBERT, LXMERT and UNITER have significantly lifted state of the art across a wide range of V+L benchmarks with joint image-text pre-training. However, little is known about the inner mechanisms that destine their impressive success. To reveal the secrets behind the scene of these powerful models, we present VALUE (Vision-And-Language Understanding Evaluation), a set of meticulously designed probing tasks (e.g., Visual Coreference Resolution, Visual Relation Detection, Linguistic Probing Tasks) generalizable to standard pre-trained V+L models, aiming to decipher the inner workings of multimodal pre-training (e.g., the implicit knowledge garnered in individual attention heads, the inherent cross-modal alignment learned through contextualized multimodal embeddings). Through extensive analysis of each archetypal model architecture via these probing tasks, our key observations are: (i) Pre-trained models exhibit a propensity for attending over text rather than images during inference. (ii) There exists a subset of attention heads that are tailored for capturing cross-modal interactions. (iii) Learned attention matrix in pre-trained models demonstrates patterns coherent with the latent alignment between image regions and textual words. (iv) Plotted attention patterns reveal visually-interpretable relations among image regions. (v) Pure linguistic knowledge is also effectively encoded in the attention heads. These are valuable insights serving to guide future work towards designing better model architecture and objectives for multimodal pre-training.

papers.title: Safety is Not Only About Refusal: Reasoning-Enhanced Fine-tuning for Interpretable LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLM safety against adversarial reasoning exploits by training models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RATIONAL, a reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to explicitly reason about safety before responding, improving robustness against adversarial reasoning exploits and providing interpretable, context-aware safety.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning (RATIONAL) enables LLMs to internalize safety-aware reasoning, improving robustness against adversarial attacks and providing interpretable, context-aware responses.
papers.key_findings:
RATIONAL reduces attack success rates on adversarial benchmarks (SorryBench, HarmBench) to very low levels.
RATIONAL generalizes to unseen attack types (gradient-based and persona-based) without direct training.
RATIONAL improves truthfulness and reduces toxicity (as shown on TruthfulQA and ToxiGen).
RATIONAL balances safety and helpfulness, reducing over-refusals on benign queries.
The ablation study shows that both reasoning and adversarial data are important: writing style attacks are mitigated by reasoning, but persuasion attacks require adversarial examples.
papers.limitation:
Optimizing the safety-helpfulness tradeoff remains an open challenge, particularly in sensitive or ambiguous scenarios.
RATIONAL primarily addresses single-turn jailbreaks but may require complementary strategies to defend against emerging attack techniques, such as adaptive multi-turn exploits.
future_direction: Improving robustness and helpfulness simultaneously via reasoning-based alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional safety alignment, which often relies on rigid refusal heuristics or representation engineering to block harmful outputs.While they are effective for direct adversarial attacks, they fall short of broader safety challenges requiring nuanced, context-aware decision-making.To address this, we propose ReAsoning-enhanced Fine-TunIng fOr iNterpretAble LLM Safety (RATIONAL), a novel framework that trains models to engage in explicit safe reasoning before response.Fine-tuned models leverage the extensive pretraining knowledge in selfgenerated reasoning to bootstrap their own safety through structured reasoning, internalizing context-sensitive decision-making.Our findings suggest that safety extends beyond refusal, requiring context awareness for more robust, interpretable, and adaptive responses.Reasoning is not only a core capability of LLMs but also a fundamental mechanism for LLM safety.RATIONAL employs reasoningenhanced fine-tuning, allowing it to reject harmful prompts while providing meaningful and context-aware responses in complex scenarios.

papers.title: How Causal Abstraction Underpins Computational Explanation
papers.research_question: What does it take for a physical system (such as a brain or neural network) to implement a given computation over suitable representational vehicles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that computational implementation should be understood through the lens of causal abstraction, specifically as an abstraction-under-translation, and explores the intertwined role of representation in this framework.
papers.conclusion: The paper offers an account of computational implementation grounded in causal abstraction and examines the role for representation in the resulting picture, arguing these issues are most profitably explored in connection with generalization and prediction.
papers.key_findings:
Computational implementation requires that the high-level computational model be an abstraction-under-translation of the low-level system.
Causal abstraction provides a precise framework for understanding how a physical system can implement an algorithm by mirroring its causal structure.
The question of admissible mappings between a system and a computational model is intertwined with questions about the place of representation in computational explanation.
Triviality arguments (e.g., that every network implements every algorithm) resurface in this causal framework, highlighting the need for further constraints on implementation.
Representational content of an internal vehicle can be captured by its causal role within a suitable abstract computational model.
papers.limitation: The proposed principle ('No Computation without Abstraction') states only a necessary condition for implementation, leaving open the need for further constraints to avoid triviality (e.g., that every network implements every algorithm).
future_direction: Further work is needed to constrain admissible translations and constructive abstractions to rule out gerrymandered implementations.
An independently motivated account of representational content could help narrow down the space of possible implementations.
papers.abstract: Explanations of cognitive behavior often appeal to computations over representations. What does it take for a system to implement a given computation over suitable representational vehicles within that system? We argue that the language of causality -- and specifically the theory of causal abstraction -- provides a fruitful lens on this topic. Drawing on current discussions in deep learning with artificial neural networks, we illustrate how classical themes in the philosophy of computation and cognition resurface in contemporary machine learning. We offer an account of computational implementation grounded in causal abstraction, and examine the role for representation in the resulting picture. We argue that these issues are most profitably explored in connection with generalization and prediction.

papers.title: Unraveling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Degradation of Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes safety alignment degradation in Vision-Language Models when vision modules are integrated, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference-time method to mitigate safety alignment degradation in VLMs by calibrating multi-modal representations to align with the LLM backbone's distribution.
papers.conclusion: CMRM effectively recovers safety alignment in VLMs without compromising performance, highlighting the importance of addressing representation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment degrades in VLMs due to representation shift when vision modality is added.
CMRM significantly reduces unsafe rates, e.g., from 61.53% to 3.15% for LLaVA-7B.
CMRM does not compromise general utility of VLMs.
The representation shift can be visualized using PCA and corrected with shifting vectors.
Full layer manipulation is optimal for safety improvement.
papers.limitation:
Increases computational overhead during inference
Focuses only on safety, not other aspects like reasoning or faithfulness
future_direction: Extend to other domains of VLMs such as reasoning ability and faithfulness
Investigate features for optimal anchor dataset
papers.abstract: The safety alignment ability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is prone to be degraded by the integration of the vision module compared to its LLM backbone. We investigate this phenomenon, dubbed as ''safety alignment degradation'' in this paper, and show that the challenge arises from the representation gap that emerges when introducing vision modality to VLMs. In particular, we show that the representations of multi-modal inputs shift away from that of text-only inputs which represent the distribution that the LLM backbone is optimized for. At the same time, the safety alignment capabilities, initially developed within the textual embedding space, do not successfully transfer to this new multi-modal representation space. To reduce safety alignment degradation, we introduce Cross-Modality Representation Manipulation (CMRM), an inference time representation intervention method for recovering the safety alignment ability that is inherent in the LLM backbone of VLMs, while simultaneously preserving the functional capabilities of VLMs. The empirical results show that our framework significantly recovers the alignment ability that is inherited from the LLM backbone with minimal impact on the fluency and linguistic capabilities of pre-trained VLMs even without additional training. Specifically, the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention. WARNING: This paper contains examples of toxic or harmful language.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Addressing divergent representations from causal interventions on neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether causal interventions on neural networks create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations and whether this affects the faithfulness of the resulting explanations to the target model in its natural state.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that causal interventions often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution, analyzes when such divergence is harmless or pernicious, and introduces a modified CL loss to mitigate pernicious divergence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that divergent representations are a common issue in causal interventions, but by understanding and mitigating them (e.g., with the CL loss), we can move towards more reliable interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, DAS) often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution.
Divergence can be harmless if it occurs in the behavioral null-space of the network layers.
Divergence can be pernicious if it activates hidden computational pathways or causes dormant behavioral changes.
The Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss can be used to reduce representational divergence in interventions while preserving behavioral accuracy.
A modified CL loss that targets causal subspaces can improve out-of-distribution intervention performance in synthetic tasks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not provide a principled, reliable method for classifying harmful divergence.
The modified CL loss is confined to a narrow set of simplistic settings and is not specific to pernicious divergence.
future_direction: Exploring ways to classify and mitigate pernicious divergence through self-supervised means
papers.abstract: A common approach to mechanistic interpretability is to causally manipulate model representations via targeted interventions in order to understand what those representations encode. Here we ask whether such interventions create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations, and whether this raises concerns about how faithful their resulting explanations are to the target model in its natural state. First, we demonstrate theoretically and empirically that common causal intervention techniques often do shift internal representations away from the natural distribution of the target model. Then, we provide a theoretical analysis of two cases of such divergences: "harmless" divergences that occur in the behavioral null-space of the layer(s) of interest, and "pernicious" divergences that activate hidden network pathways and cause dormant behavioral changes. Finally, in an effort to mitigate the pernicious cases, we apply and modify the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss from Grant (2025) allowing representations from causal interventions to remain closer to the natural distribution, reducing the likelihood of harmful divergences while preserving the interpretive power of the interventions. Together, these results highlight a path towards more reliable interpretability methods.

papers.title: What changed? Investigating Debiasing Methods using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: Why do debiasing methods have varying impacts on downstream tasks, and how do they affect internal components of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Debiasing methods impact language models by concentrating changes in the first two layers and attention heads, and their effectiveness depends on the bias metric used.
